source_text: Ἵν' οὖν μέσην βαδίσω τοῦ καιροῦ, καὶ τοῦ πό θου τῶν ἀκουόντων, οὕτω μοι δοκεῖ ποιητέον εἶναι· τὰ μὲν ἄλλα παρεῖναι τοῖς εἰδόσιν, ἐκδιδάσκειν τοὺς ἀγνοοῦντας, εἴπερ εἰσί τινες, ἵν' ἀμφότεροι εὐεργετῶνται ὁμοίως, καὶ οἱ διδάσκοντες τὰ ἐκείνου, καὶ οἱ μανθάνοντες (ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὸ μεμνῆσθαι τοῦ ἀν δρὸς, ἁγιασμὸς, καὶ μέγιστον εἰς παράκλησιν ἀρε τῆς ὁ λόγος)· ἑνὸς δὲ ἢ δύο τῶν ἐκείνου διὰ βραχέων ἐπιμνησθῆναι, καὶ τούτων ὅσα μηδὲ βουλομένῳ παρ ελθεῖν δυνατόν. Ηʹ. Μνησθήσομαι δὲ τοῦ προτέρου βίου, καὶ ἥτις αὐτῷ γέγονε σωτηρίας ὁδὸς, καὶ τίς ἡ κλῆσις, καὶ ἡ πρὸς τὸ κρεῖττον μετάθεσις. Ἐκεῖνο μέν γε λίαν ἀγεννὲς καὶ μικρόψυχον, οἴεσθαι καθυβρίζεσθαι τὸν ἀθλητὴν τῇ μνήμῃ τῶν σκαιοτέρων. Ἐπεὶ οὕτω καὶ Παῦλος ἡμῖν οὐκ ἐπαινετὸς ὁ μέγας, καὶ Ματθαῖος ὁ τελώνης ἐν τοῖς κακίστοις, καὶ Κυπριανὸς αὐτός· ὁ μὲν τῶν προτέρων ἑαυτοῦ διωγμῶν μεμνημένος, καὶ τῆς τοῦ ζήλου μεταθέσεως, ἵν' ἐκ τοῦ παραλλήλου μᾶλλον δοξάσῃ τὸν εὐεργέτην· ὁ δὲ τὸν Τελώνην ἑαυτῷ προστιθεὶς ἐν τῇ τῶν μαθητῶν ἀπ αριθμήσει, ὥσπερ ἄλλο τι τῶν τιμίων ἐπίσημον· ὁ δὲ καὶ μακρῷ λόγῳ στηλιτεύων τὴν προτέραν ἑαυτοῦ κακίαν, ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο Θεῷ καρποφορήσῃ, τὴν ἐξαγόρευσιν, καὶ πολλοῖς ὁδὸς γένηται τῆς χρηστοτέρας ἐλπίδος τῶν ἀπὸ κακίας ἐπιστρεφόντων. Τίς οὖν ἡ κακία, καὶ σκοπεῖτε, ὅση καὶ ἡλίκη τὸ μέγεθος· Δαιμόνων ἦν θεραπευτὴς, ὁ Χριστοῦ μαθητὴς ὕστερον· καὶ διώκτης πικρότατος, ὁ μέγας τῆς ἀληθείας ἀγωνιστής· καὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ταράσσων τὴν ἡμε τέραν ὁδὸν, διὰ τὸ ἐν ἀμφοτέροις κράτος, ὁ κρά τιστος ἀμφότερα μετὰ τοῦτο Χριστιανοῖς. Ὅσον κα κὸν καὶ γοητεία τούτοις προστιθεμένη, τῶν ἐκεί νου τὸ γνωριμώτατον! ὅσῳ δεινότερον καὶ ἀπληστία σώματος, ἣ καὶ τοὺς τἄλλα σοφοὺς ἐκμαίνειν δύναται, καὶ χεῖρον φρονεῖν βιάζεται, καθά περ ὑβριστὴς πῶλος, τὸν λογισμὸν συναρπάζουσα! Θʹ. Ἥκει δὲ ἡμῖν ἐπ' αὐτὸ τὸ κεφάλαιον ὁ λόγος. Καὶ μὴ πρὸς τὰ πρῶτά τις ὁρῶν Κυπριανοῦ, ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ἐφιέτω· τοῖς δὲ τελευταίοις σωφρονιζέσθω. Παρθένος τις ἦν τῶν εὐπατρίδων, καὶ κοσμίων. Ἀκούετε, παρθένοι, καὶ συναγάλλεσθε, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ τῶν ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ὅσαι σώφρονές τε καὶ φιλοσώφρονες· κοινὸν γὰρ ἀμφοτέραις καλλώπισμα τὸ διήγημα. Καὶ ἡ παρθένος καλὴ τῷ εἴδει σφόδρα· προσᾳδέτω ταύτῃ μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ θεῖος Δαβὶδ, Πᾶσα ἡ δόξα, λέγων, τῆς θυγατρὸς τοῦ βασιλέως ἔσω θεν, νύμφη Χριστοῦ γνησία, κάλλος ἀπόθετον, ἄγαλμα ἔμψυχον, ἀνάθημα ἄσυλον, τέμενος ἀνεπίβατον, κῆπος κεκλεισμένος, πηγὴ ἐσφραγισμένη (προσᾳδέτω γάρ τι καὶ Σολομὼν), μόνῳ Χριστῷ τηρουμένη. Ταύτης ὁ μέγας ἥλω Κυπριανὸς, οὐκ οἶδ' ὅθεν καὶ ὅπως, τῆς πάντα ἀσφαλοῦς καὶ κοσμίας. Ψαύουσι γὰρ ὀφθαλμοὶ λίχνοι καὶ τῶν ἀψαύστων, τὸ προχειρότατον ὀργάνων καὶ ἀπληστότατον. Καὶ οὐχ ἥλω μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπείρα. Ὢ τῆς εὐηθείας, εἰ ταύτην συλήσειν ἤλπιζε, μᾶλλον δὲ τῆς ἀναισχυντίας τοῦ τὰ τοιαῦτα τολμῶντός τε καὶ τολμᾷν πείθοντος! Ἐκεῖνος καὶ εἰς τὸν παράδεισον ἀπ' ἀρχῆς παρέδυ κατὰ τοῦ πρώτου πλάσματος· καὶ μέσος ἀγγέλων ἵσταται τὸν Ἰὼβ ἐξαιτήσων· καὶ τὸ τελευταῖον, κατ' αὐτοῦ τολμᾷ τοῦ Δεσπότου, τοῦ καταλύσοντος αὐτὸν καὶ θανατώσοντος, καὶ πεῖραν προσάγει τῷ ἀπειράστῳ (ἐπειδὴ δεύτερον Ἀδὰμ εἶδε τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸ φαινόμενον), ὡς καὶ τοῦτον καταπαλαίσων.
thought_title: Cyprian's evil past and the virgin who resisted him
orientation: Gregory pauses his praise of Cyprian's eloquence to tell new hearers about Cyprian's earlier life as a worshipper of demons and persecutor and about the noble virgin whose resistance led toward his conversion.
pass_a_gloss: So that I may walk a middle course between the occasion and the desire of the hearers, it seems to me that this must be done. To pass over the other things for those who know them, and to teach them fully to those who do not know, if there are any such, so that both may be benefited in like manner, both those who teach the things of that man and those who learn, since also the remembrance of the man is consecration, and the discourse is very great toward exhortation to virtue. But to make mention in few words of one or two of the things of that man, and of these as many as are not possible to pass over even for one who wishes it. I will make mention of his former way of life, and what road to salvation came to be for him, and what his calling was, and his conversion toward the better. That at least is very base and small souled, to suppose that the athlete is insulted by remembrance of the more awkward things. For otherwise also Paul the great is not praiseworthy for us, and Matthew the collector of tax is among the worst, and Cyprian himself. The one remembering his own former persecutions and the conversion of his zeal, so that from the comparison he may glorify the benefactor more. The other adding to himself the collector of tax in the numbering of the disciples, as some other honorable distinction among honorable things. And the other even with a long discourse exposing to public shame his own former evil, so that he may bear fruit with this also for God, his open confession, and may become for many a road of better hope, for those turning back from evil. What then was the evil, and observe how great and how large in greatness. He was a server of demons, the man who later became a disciple of Christ. And a most bitter persecutor, the man who became a great champion of the truth. And disturbing our way by word and by deed, through his power in both, the man who after this became strongest in both for Christians. What a great evil also sorcery added to these, the most well known thing of his things. And how more terrible bodily greed, which is able to madden even those wise in other things, and forces them to think worse, seizing reason together with itself as a wanton colt does. The discourse has come for us to the chief point itself. And let no one looking to the earlier things of Cyprian rush toward pleasures. But let him be made to practice self control by the last things. There was a certain virgin of the well born and orderly women. Hear, virgins, and rejoice together, but rather also as many under the yoke as are self controlled and lovers of self control. For the narrative is a common boast for both. And the virgin was very beautiful in form. Let the divine David join in song to her with us, saying, All the glory of the daughter of the king is within, true bride of Christ, beauty laid up in store, living statue, offering that none may violate, sanctuary that none may enter, garden shut, fountain sealed, for let Solomon also join in song in some part, the woman kept for Christ alone. By her the great Cyprian was caught, I know not from where and how, by her who was secure in all things and orderly. For lustful eyes touch even untouched things, the handiest of organs and the most greedy. And Cyprian was not only caught, but the devil also made an attempt. O his folly, if he hoped that he would plunder her, but rather O the shamelessness of the one both daring such things and persuading to dare. That one even from the beginning crept into the paradise against the first fashioned man. And he stands in the midst of angels asking to have Job. And at the last, he dares against the Master himself, the one who will destroy him and put him to death, and he brings trial to the one who cannot be tried, since he saw the appearing of God as a second Adam, as if he would wrestle down even this one.

choices.why: ἐπεὶ is causal, and οὕτω points back to supposing insult; keeps the cause for Paul, Matthew, Cyprian losing praise.
Superlative adjective with neuter article marks what most marked Cyprian, not a moral rank among deeds.

choices.term: οὐχ ἥλω μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπείρα
choices.english: Cyprian was not only caught, but the devil also made an attempt
choices.why: ἥλω is passive of Cyprian being caught in desire, while ἐπείρα is active attempt by the tempter named next as daring and persuading.
rejected: he was not only captured, but he made an attempt

pass_b_english: To hold a middle course between the occasion and the longing of my hearers, this seems to me the right thing to do: to leave the rest to those who know it, and to instruct those who do not, if there are any, so that both sides receive the same benefit, those who teach Cyprian's deeds and those who learn them, since even remembering the man is sanctification, and my speech is the greatest encouragement to virtue. But I shall touch briefly on one or two of his deeds, and only those which no one could pass over even if he wished.

I shall mention his former life, and what road brought him salvation, and what his calling was, and his conversion toward the better. It would be utterly base and small-minded to suppose that the athlete is insulted by remembering his baser days. For otherwise even Paul the great would not deserve our praise, Matthew the tax collector would be ranked among the worst, and so would Cyprian himself. Paul remembered his own former persecutions, and the conversion of his zeal, so that by the contrast he might glorify his benefactor all the more. Matthew adds the Tax Collector to his own name in numbering the disciples, as if it were some other honorable distinction. And Cyprian himself holds his own former wickedness up to public shame in a long account, so that even his confession may bear fruit for God, and he may become for many who turn from wickedness a road toward better hope.

Consider, then, what that wickedness was, and how great its magnitude. He who later became a disciple of Christ had been a servant of demons. He who became a great champion of the truth had been a most bitter persecutor. He who afterward was mightiest in both for Christians had troubled our way in both word and deed, through his power in both. And add to these the evil of sorcery, the most well known thing about him. Add too bodily lust, more terrible still, which can madden even men wise in all else and forces them to think basely, snatching reason away like an unruly colt.

But my story now reaches its very head. Let no one look to Cyprian's beginnings and set his heart on pleasures; let him learn self-control from Cyprian's end. There was a virgin of noble and modest birth. Listen, virgins, and rejoice with her, and even more all you married women who are self-controlled and love self-control, for this story adorns you both alike. And the virgin was very beautiful in appearance. Let the divine David sing of her with us, saying, "All the glory of the king's daughter is within" (Psalm 45:13), a true bride of Christ, beauty set apart, a living statue, an inviolable offering, an untrodden sanctuary, kept for Christ alone. Let Solomon too add his verse, "a garden locked, a spring sealed" (Song of Songs 4:12).

Great Cyprian was caught by her, though she was in all things secure and modest, and I do not know from where or how. For greedy eyes touch even what must not be touched, the readiest of organs and the most insatiable. Cyprian was not only caught, but he also made an attempt on her. What folly, if Cyprian hoped to plunder her, and what shamelessness rather in the one who both dares such things and persuades men to dare them. That devil from the beginning slipped into paradise against the first creature, and he stands in the midst of angels to demand Job, and at the last he dares against the Master himself, who will destroy him and put him to death, and he brings trial upon the One who cannot be tried, since he saw God's visible presence as a second Adam, as if he would wrestle even him to the ground.

problems.quote: Cyprian was not only caught, but the devil also made an attempt.
problems.source_quote: Καὶ οὐχ ἥλω μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπείρα.
problems.why: The subject of ἐπείρα is still Cyprian: he was not only captivated but also tried to seduce her. The English introduces the devil as a new agent here.
problems.fix: He was not only caught; he also made an attempt on her.

problems.quote: nor Matthew the tax collector, though ranked among the worst, nor Cyprian himself
problems.source_quote: καὶ Ματθαῖος ὁ τελώνης ἐν τοῖς κακίστοις, καὶ Κυπριανὸς αὐτός
problems.why: ἐν τοῖς κακίστοις is the absurd result of that view, not a fact about Matthew.
problems.fix: Paul the great would not deserve our praise, Matthew the tax collector would be ranked among the worst, and so would Cyprian himself.
problems.ruling: Syntax: 'οὕτω... οὐκ ἐπαινετὸς ὁ μέγας... καὶ Ματθαῖος ἐν τοῖς κακίστοις' is the absurd consequence of the view; English wrongly states Matthew was ranked among the worst.

problems.quote: Great Cyprian was caught by her, though so secure and modest in all things
problems.source_quote: Ταύτης ὁ μέγας ἥλω Κυπριανός, οὐκ οἶδ' ὅθεν καὶ ὅπως, τῆς πάντα ἀσφαλοῦς καὶ κοσμίας
problems.why: The feminine genitive describes the virgin, not Cyprian, as wholly secure and modest.
problems.fix: Great Cyprian was caught by her—I know not whence or how—though she was in all things secure and modest.
problems.ruling: τῆς πάντα ἀσφαλοῦς καὶ κοσμίας is feminine genitive, describing the virgin ('her, so secure and modest'), not Cyprian; English misattributes it to Cyprian.

problems.quote: He who after his conversion served Christians most fully in both word and deed
problems.source_quote: ὁ κράτιστος ἀμφότερα μετὰ τοῦτο Χριστιανοῖς
problems.why: κράτιστος means he was afterward mightiest in both for Christians, not that he served them.
problems.fix: He who was afterward mightiest in both for Christians had troubled our way in word and deed, through his power in both.
problems.ruling: ὁ κράτιστος ἀμφότερα μετὰ τοῦτο Χριστιανοῖς means 'mightiest in both for Christians'; 'served Christians most fully' changes the sense, and parallels κράτος just before.

fixed: agency: subject of ὲπείρα is still Cyprian, not the devil; fixed to he also made an attempt on her.
mistranslation: ἐν τοῖς κακίστοις is conditional result under οὕτω, not fact; fixed to would be ranked.
agency: τῆς πάντα ἀσφαλοῦς καὶ κοσμίας is feminine agreeing with Ταύτης, the virgin; fixed to she was secure and modest.
mistranslation: ὁ κράτιστος ἀμφότερα μετἀ τοῦτο Χριστιανοῖς means mightiest in both for Christians, not served; fixed accordingly.

last_rejected.source_quote: Παρθένος τις ἦν τῶν εὐπατριδῶν, καὶ κοσμίων
last_rejected.why: κοσμίων means decorous or respectable, not low birth. “Modest birth” suggests humble origin and clashes with noble birth.
last_rejected.fix: There was a virgin of noble family and of decorous life.
last_rejected.ruling: κοσμίων means orderly or decorous. 'Modest' is within its normal range, and 'noble and modest birth' is a slightly loose but acceptable rendering of τῶν εὐπατριδῶν, καὶ κοσμίων.

last_rejected.quote: Let no one look to Cyprian's beginnings and set his heart on pleasures
last_rejected.source_quote: μὴ πρὸς τὰ πρῶτά τις ὁρῶν Κυπριανοῦ, ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ἐφιέτω
last_rejected.why: The prohibition is on desiring pleasures while looking at the early life. English also forbids looking.
last_rejected.fix: Let no one, looking at Cyprian's beginnings, set his heart on pleasures; let him learn self-control from the end.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Let no one look to Cyprian's beginnings and set his heart on pleasures' follows μὴ ... τις ὁρῶν ... ἐφιέτω: the negation covers the person looking and desiring. The meaning is preserved.
